The problem

Fast Credit had branches, customers, and zero digital presence.

Customers were driving to physical offices to apply for loans, check balances, and start investments. Competitors were shipping mobile apps. The company needed to move — fast.

The brief said "build a mobile banking app." The hard problem nobody had written down was different: how do you onboard Nigerian users into a CBN-regulated financial product without losing them before they get their first loan?

Research & discovery

250+ alpha user sessions before a single screen went to engineering.

The sessions covered first-time app users, salary earners, market traders, and civil servants — the real Fast Credit customer base. The biggest friction point surfaced immediately: the KYC wall.

"I don't want to give my BVN to an app I don't trust yet. What if something goes wrong? Can I call someone?" — Tunde Adeyemi, 34, civil servant, Lagos · First-time fintech user

The original flow demanded full KYC — BVN, NIN, proof of address, employment details — before a user could access any feature. Drop-off was catastrophic in testing. Users weren't refusing to provide information; they were refusing to provide everything before the app had earned a single moment of trust.

The advocacy moment

When the research said the brief was wrong, I called the meeting.

This is where the design work became a leadership challenge. The original PRD specified a single-gate KYC flow — standard for regulated products. My research said this would kill onboarding. I scheduled time with the PM, Head of Engineering, and senior stakeholders.

I presented the data: drop-off points from alpha sessions, quotes from real users, and a proposed progressive 3-tier KYC system that stayed fully within CBN compliance while dramatically reducing upfront friction.

The solution — Progressive 3-Tier KYC
Tier 1 (phone number only): User gets access, can explore the app and see their potential loan limits. Trust is built before documents are asked for.

Tier 2 (BVN + basic details): Unlocks transfers up to ₦50,000/day and basic savings. User sees clear value before going deeper.

Tier 3 (full KYC): Unlocks full loan access, high transfer limits, and investment products. By this point the user has experienced the product and trusts it.

The team restructured the entire PRD around this model. Engineering rebuilt the verification pipeline. It shipped.

Wireframes

Every edge case designed before the visuals.

Low-to-high fidelity wireframes mapped the full onboarding flow — splash, phone verification, OTP, dashboard. Each state handled the messy reality: number already registered, checkbox not ticked, loading state, BVN validation in progress.

Wireframe flows — onboarding, OTP, dashboard entry

Final product

Four modules. One unified product.

The shipped app covers Home, Investments, Loans, and a More settings panel with account upgrade. Each screen was built for real Nigerian mobile conditions — variable connectivity, older devices, users making real financial decisions.

Investment
Loan

A/B testing & iteration

Four screens, eight variants, measured decisions.

During alpha, four screens showed friction. I tested two variants per screen and made data-informed decisions before launch.

A/B Testing — Dashboard, Transaction History, Transfer Money, Loan Screen
Dashboard
A: Minimal white layout, icon-only actions, no context.
B: Green hero card, Withdraw/Fund CTAs surfaced, full recent transactions, SME Loan banner. Users oriented faster and engaged more features on first session.
Transaction History
A: Date-grouped list only.
B: Added search by bank/account, filter tabs (All/Transfer/Received/Reversal), calendar filter. Turned a passive log into an active lookup tool.
Transfer Money
A: Two large icon buttons. Extra tap, no context.
B: Top toggle, recent beneficiary avatars, source account, daily limit, remark field. Reduced friction before commitment.
Loan Screen — the biggest shift
A: Red "Apply Now" CTA centred. No repayment breakdown, no progress, no top-up. Users felt uncertain.

B: Outstanding balance at top, active loan broken down (amount, tenor, progress 3 of 12, monthly repayment, status). Top-Up Loan for existing borrowers. Red CTA replaced with brand green — anxiety reduced, trust increased. A prompt became a financial management tool.
Outcome

10,000 users in the first weeks. 80% onboarded on first attempt.

The remaining 20% who didn't complete on first attempt were blocked by a systemic BVN mismatch between their registered details and the CBN database — a data quality issue outside the product's control. That distinction mattered: it kept the team focused on the right problem.

The progressive KYC system is now the backbone of the product's onboarding architecture. The design system I built — components, tokens, spacing, interaction patterns — reduced design-to-dev handoff time by 90% and became the foundation for every subsequent feature shipped.

Post-launch iteration

Then real usage exposed a failure the tiers couldn't fix.

Progressive KYC solved the trust problem. But once real users hit the BVN upgrade at volume, a second failure surfaced — quieter, and almost invisible in a demo. The flow asked people to type their name alongside their BVN, then matched the two. A real slice of Nigerians can't pass that match through no fault of their own: women who've married and taken a new name but haven't updated their BVN, people whose BVN carries a legal name they never actually use, small differences in spelling or word order. The system read every one of these as a mismatch and silently blocked the upgrade.

"My BVN still has my maiden name. The app keeps telling me my details don't match — but they are mine." — Recurring theme across post-launch support tickets

The fix came from inverting the principle: don't make users prove what the BVN already knows. Instead of typing details to be matched against a record, the user provides their BVN alone, verifies they own it, and confirms what we pull back. The name is never typed — so it can never mismatch.

1
Enter BVN
One field. Nothing to type by hand, nothing to mistype.
2
Verify ownership
A one-time code is sent to the phone number tied to that BVN.
3
Confirm details
We show the name and data pulled from the BVN — the user confirms it's them.
4
Liveness check
A quick selfie confirms a real person matches the verified BVN.
5
Set PIN & password
Secure the account. Upgrade complete.
Why the inversion works
The old flow made the user responsible for a data record they don't control. The new flow makes the BVN the source of truth and the user the confirmer — not the data-entry clerk. It also turns a dry compliance step into a trust moment: the user sees exactly what data is being used, and agrees to it, before going any further.

Removing the manual name-match — the single biggest silent failure point in the upgrade — cut failed account upgrades by roughly 70% and shortened the journey. People stopped being locked out over a name they were never able to change.

~70%
Fewer failed KYC upgrades
1 field
BVN only — no name to mismatch
5 steps
End-to-end account upgrade
The edge we're designing for next

One group the BVN-first flow still can't fully reach.

Pull-and-confirm removed the name mismatch — but it leans on one assumption: that the user can still receive a code on the phone number tied to their BVN. In practice, a real slice can't. Numbers registered years ago by an enrolment agent, SIMs long since swapped or lost — some users don't even know which number their BVN carries. We monitor this closely and fund it, so OTP delivery-and-entry friction sits at a managed ~7–8% rather than locking people out. But 7–8% of onboarding is still real people — and it lands on the same group progressive KYC was built to protect.

So the next move isn't another screen. It's a research-backed proposal to make verification lean less on a number the user can't control, and to open a route for people whose BVN phone is unreachable — without loosening a single CBN requirement. That work is underway now: quantifying the failure, mapping exactly who it hits, and testing an easier path to a verified account.

How it started

I was walking past a conversation. An hour later I had the audit.

Marketing was frustrated the website wasn't converting. Sales said leads were coming in confused about what Fast Credit actually offered. Nobody had a plan to fix it.

I ran an independent audit that evening. Within an hour I had a clear picture: the site wasn't just outdated — it had structural problems no amount of visual polish would fix. I scheduled time with leadership the next week with findings and a proposal.

Before — the 6 failures

Every failure was structural. None could be solved by repainting.

Before — five separate sparse pages, no hierarchy, weak CTAs
Failure 01
Not modern. Visual design hadn't kept pace with the brand. Trust signals absent. First impressions cost the business before a word was read.
Failure 02
Inefficient navigation. Five separate product pages (Loans, Investments, Fast Thrift, Public Workers, BNPL). Users clicked through a maze to understand the offering.
Failure 03
Cognitive overload. Every page tried to explain everything. No hierarchy. Users couldn't identify what to do next at any point in the journey.
Failure 04
Too many sparse pages. Content was spread thin. Pages that needed depth were empty. Pages that needed consolidation were siloed.
Failure 05
Irrelevant imagery. Stock photos had no connection to the Fast Credit brand or customer. Visual language undermining trust instead of building it.
Failure 06
Poor layout & composition. No consistent grid. Arbitrary spacing. Visual rhythm broken on every page. Site looked assembled in parts.
Wireframes & IA

Collapse five sparse pages into one purposeful structure.

The first design decision was structural: consolidated navigation. Every product had to earn its place in the hierarchy. I also added a loan calculator — something no stakeholder had asked for, but that every user needed to make a decision.

Desktop and mobile wireframes — restructured IA, new loan calculator
Final design

A homepage that actually tells the story.

Hero with clear value proposition. Trust signals upfront — CBN licensed, Bbb rated by Augusto & Co. App download CTAs surfaced. Product cards consolidated. Benefits explained. Testimonials and partners as social proof. The whole page reads in one scroll.

Shipped homepage — hero, products, benefits, testimonials, partners, CTA footer
Full site

Every page rebuilt — including one nobody asked for.

The redesign covered the full site: About, all loan product pages, the custom loan calculator, blog, and contact pages with office locations. Designed at desktop and mobile breakpoints.

Full site — About, Loans, Fast Pearl, Calculator, Blog, Contact
Outcome

70% engagement lift. The unrequested calculator became the highest-engaged element.

Engagement rose 70%. Bounce rate dropped. Lead quality improved — sales reported customers now arrived already understanding what they were applying for.

The loan calculator was never in the brief because nobody thought to put it there. That's the work I find most valuable: the thing that wasn't assigned but needed to exist.

The problem

Strong product. Liability of a website.

Evamor Water is a premium Nigerian dispensable water brand — alkaline, BPA-free, 5-gallon bottles serving health-conscious consumers, offices, hotels, and restaurants across Lagos. The product was excellent. The website was the bottleneck.

Problem 01
Broken navigation. Users couldn't find Order Now without already knowing it existed. The IA assumed familiarity the user didn't have.
Problem 02
Weak mobile responsiveness. Majority of Nigerian web traffic is mobile. The site existed on mobile but it broke under the weight of awkward layouts, mistuned touch targets, and inconsistent typography.
Problem 03
Friction-heavy checkout. Form asked too much, too early, with no context about delivery or pricing. Users abandoned before submission.
Sitemap & wireframes

The conversion path: one click from anywhere.

Restructured the site around the user's primary intent: understand the product, trust the brand, place an order. New sitemap put the conversion path one click from anywhere on the site.

Wireframes — Home, About, Products, Order form · Desktop + Mobile
Visual identity

Deep ocean blues. Trust, by association.

Palette built around deep ocean blues — communicating purity, quality, and trust. Poppins for its clean neutrality. The Order Now CTA persistent across every page.

Before — the gap

All the ingredients of a premium brand. A template undermining all of it.

Ceedaa had 20+ years of operation, NAFDAC and SON certifications, a loyal regional customer base across Ogun State, and a product line that genuinely deserved shelf space next to national players. The website was the one thing working against them.

Before — generic template, flat identity, no emotional pull, no mobile
Problem 01
No brand identity. Generic pink hero with a slider. Nothing communicated premium quality, Nigerian heritage, or the brand's 20-year story.
Problem 02
No mobile design. Nigerian FMCG buyers research on mobile — especially for home delivery products. Desktop-only meant invisible to most of the audience.
Problem 03
Weak product presentation. Good photography existed but was buried in a basic grid with no hierarchy, no variant exploration, no story around why the product was worth choosing.
Problem 04
No brand narrative. About section was factual but cold. No vision or mission landing emotionally. Core values not communicated in a way that built connection.
Design decisions

Evolution, not revolution. Elevate the brand, don't replace it.

Brief was brand elevation — not a new brand. Existing colours (red, white) kept but refined into a deliberate palette with a warm off-white base that let product photography breathe. Urbanist chosen for confident geometry and premium feel without being cold.
